newsitem.title: NORWAY: Computer theft claims rising, say cargo insurers.
newsitem.headline: Computer theft claims rising, say cargo insurers.

text.p: Thefts of computer parts and memory chips have soared, leaving insurers around the world stuck for a solution to rising claims.

Cargo insurance associations from around the world have reported substantial increases in thefts and non-delivery of shipments, mostly from air and overland routes, to the International Union of Marine Insurers (IUMI) which met in Oslo today.
The problem stems from high global demand for computers, parts and particulary memory chips, which makes it easy for them to re-enter the production chain.
Insurers are concerned that their high value, compared to the very low recovery from cargo carriers, is leaving them with massive claims bills.
IUMI member associations reported 26 single incidents last year where the loss was worth more than $200,000, and some went as high as $1.5 million.

Australia reported several losses in the A$50,000-A$100,000 bracket involving computer components stolen during air transport via Taipei and Hong Kong. These incidents appeared to involve airport officials, the insurers said.
Other airports targetted by computer thieves include Heathrow, Johannesburg International and Amsterdam.

In an attempt to solve the problem, insurers are encouraging greater use of non-descriptive labelling on packages, coded markings changed regularly to deter thieves from pilfering packages with unknown content and the installation of satellite tracking devices for vehicles carrying such cargoes.
Other suggestions include welding the doors of containers and employing armed guards. But none are sure to be implemented or to curb the massive increase.
"It really is a problem which shows no signs of abating and in the U.S. in particular single claims can easily exceed $1 million," one insurer said.

"It should really be up to the carriers to do more, and for exporters to avoid trans-shipment and employ greater secrecy. After encouragement to take preventative action, insurers can do little more than increase deductibles and premiums," the insurer said.
